metadata.title: Is Claude's DCF Number Its Own Judgment?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude's DCF valuation reflects its own judgment about what a company is worth, or is running a fixed formula over the assumptions it was given. Lands the carry-out that a DCF number is Claude running your growth and discount-rate assumptions through a fixed formula -- not Claude's opinion of what a company is worth.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks whether Claude's DCF model reflects its own judgment about what a company is worth. It doesn't. Liam is here to take you through what the skill actually computes, step by step.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What decides what it's worth -- judgment?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'the formula', lands the real question

props.text:
What decides
what it's worth —
judgment?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'the formula') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess is that Claude's valuation reflects its own judgment about the company -- like an analyst who's studied the business and reached a conclusion. But the skill doesn't have an opinion. It takes the assumptions it's given -- a growth rate, a discount rate, a terminal growth rate -- and runs them through a fixed formula. Feed it a different assumption and the valuation moves without protest; it never argues that your number is wrong.

shot.new_visual_element: An analyst figure weighing a conclusion, struck through; assumptions feeding a formula box, lit

production_viz.label: Judgment, struck -- formula, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'ANALYST JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble arriving at a single conclusion mark. Right: three input tags -- 'GROWTH RATE', 'DISCOUNT RATE', 'TERMINAL GROWTH' -- feeding into a card labelled 'FORMULA'. The analyst side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the formula side stays lit. A changed input tag flows into the formula and a small output number changes with it -- no protest, no pause.

beats.narration_text: What the skill actually does is project each year's cash flow forward, then discount every one of them -- plus a terminal value -- back to today, using one number: the discount rate, WACC. Watch the anchor: turn that one dial, and the valuation follows it, every time.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a discount-rate dial wired directly to a single valuation readout

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one dial, one number
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A row of projected cash-flow bars (years 1-5) plus a 'TERMINAL VALUE' bar, all feeding down into a dial labelled 'DISCOUNT RATE (WACC)'. The dial connects by a single line to a readout card labelled 'INTRINSIC VALUE'. The dial is turned up; the readout number visibly drops in response. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, AS A GRID, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That's the same dial a sensitivity analysis turns, again and again, watching the valuation swing. A number that swings a lot for a small change in the discount rate doesn't mean the model is broken -- the input was never precise to begin with. And a valuation that holds steady across the sensitivity range doesn't prove it's right either -- the terminal value, which usually carries most of the total, is still just a guess about the distant future.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS as a sensitivity grid, then splits into 'swings a lot is not broken' and 'holds steady is not right'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- sensitivity grid, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIAL-AND-READOUT COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical placement, now repeated three times side by side as a small sensitivity grid -- same dial, three settings, three readout numbers, each visibly different. It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left shows the readout numbers spread far apart, labelled 'swings a lot is not broken'; right shows a separate 'TERMINAL VALUE' bar sized far larger than the yearly cash-flow bars beside it, labelled 'holds steady is not right'.

beats.narration_text: A DCF number is Claude running your growth and discount-rate assumptions through a fixed formula -- not Claude's opinion of what a company is worth. Change the assumption, and the number moves.

props.quote: A DCF number is Claude running your growth and discount-rate assumptions through a fixed formula — not Claude's opinion of what a company is worth. Change the assumption, and the number moves.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt -- read it with me. Give Claude a simple set of DCF assumptions -- a growth rate, a discount rate, a terminal growth rate -- and ask it to run the dcf-model skill and value a hypothetical company. Then change only the discount rate by one point and watch how far the number moves. That's the fastest way to see how much of the valuation is assumption, not analysis. Liam, in for Bear.
